issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by high threat perception, safety behaviors, severe hopelessness, and a robbery-related fear structure. A patient who is persistently choosing safe seats and feeling intensely endangered would more plausibly show avoidance/hypervigilance than generalized risk-taking; this reads as an opposing clinical state within the Threat node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is a weak fit for mugging/robbery trauma in this profile. There is no supporting trigger, memory, or appraisal content involving police, security staff, uniforms, or institutional betrayal, so this strategy targets a symptom context not otherwise represented in the formulation. For this trauma type, avoiding authority/uniformed people is not impossible, but here it lacks clinical linkage and appears incoherent with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
It was a Tuesday night in late October when Leo was leaving the hospital after a double shift. He was a nurse on the cardiac floor, accustomed to long hours and the quiet hum of empty corridors. That night, as he walked through the poorly lit parking garage, a man stepped out from behind a pillar and pressed a knife to his ribs. The mugging lasted less than a minute—his wallet, his phone, his watch—but the image of the blade, the cold pressure against his skin, and the sound of his own breath catching in his throat became etched into his mind with a clarity that felt like a curse. He could still see the man’s eyes, the flicker of the fluorescent light on the steel, the exact angle of the hand that held the weapon. When the memory returned, which it did many times a day, he would feel a sharp, stabbing pain in his right side, exactly where the knife had pressed. It was as if his body had not understood that the event was over. In the weeks that followed, Leo began to believe that there was something fundamentally wrong with him—an intrinsic fault that had made him a target. He replayed the moment again and again, searching for what he could have done differently, and each time the conclusion was the same: he had been weak, he had been careless, and something about him had invited the attack. This belief began to shape everything. He became convinced that nothing good could happen to him anymore, that his future had been stolen along with his wallet. He would catch himself staring at the ceiling at 3 a.m., unable to sleep, the image of the knife flashing behind his eyelids, and he would think, *This is what I deserve.*

Because he believed the world was now fundamentally dangerous and that he was somehow marked, Leo started scanning every environment he entered. At work, he would check the mirrors in the medication room twice before opening the door. He chose his seat in the break room based on how protected he felt—always with his back to the wall, always facing the door. Walking to his car, he looked behind him constantly, sometimes stopping and turning around fully to check if anyone was following. These habits were exhausting, but they felt necessary. He also began keeping his mind occupied all the time—listening to podcasts during every spare moment, working extra shifts, volunteering for tasks no one else wanted. He told himself it was productivity, but the real reason was that silence gave the memory room to return. But the more he threw himself into distraction, the more the memory seemed to ambush him during the quiet moments he tried so hard to eliminate, as if the effort of keeping it at bay had only kept it waiting just beneath the surface. The more he tried to distract himself, the more the images seemed to intrude, as if his mind was punishing him for trying to escape. The pain in his side would flare up during these moments, a vivid physical echo that reinforced his sense that the event was not over, that it was still happening to him. His wife noticed the change. He stopped sitting with her on the couch, preferring the chair by the door. He would flinch when she touched his right side. She asked what was wrong, and he said he was just tired, but the truth was that he felt a deep, gnawing hopelessness. He could not imagine a future where he felt safe again, and he was certain that no amount of vigilance would ever be enough. The checking, the scanning, the distraction—none of it made him feel better. It only reminded him that he was always on guard, always afraid, and that the man with the knife was still there, in his mind, pressing against his ribs. What finally brought Leo to seek help was a moment in the break room at work. A colleague touched his shoulder from behind to ask him a question, and Leo spun around, his hand raised, his heart pounding. The look of shock on his colleague’s face was the moment he realized he could no longer manage this alone. He was terrified that he would lose his job, his marriage, his sense of himself. But more than that, he was afraid that he would never stop looking over his shoulder, that the memory would never fade, and that the man in the garage had taken more than his wallet—he had taken the person Leo used to be. Each time he had to resort to another podcast or another extra shift to keep the memory at bay, he felt the quiet confirmation that he was indeed too fragile to face his own mind — that something must be fundamentally broken in him if he needed this much effort just to get through an ordinary day.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies (distraction, hypervigilance) influence or lead to the intrusive memory; instead, the memory triggers the strategies.
No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies (distraction, hypervigilance) cause or reinforce negative appraisals; the appraisals appear as preceding beliefs.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies (distraction, hypervigilance) influence or lead to the intrusive memory; instead, the memory triggers the strategies.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies (distraction, hypervigilance) cause or reinforce negative appraisals; the appraisals appear as preceding beliefs.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
